en: Or perhaps it was Badirek.
The dominion of earth and water,
Was he one whom the earth itself touched?
Kaisan kept him captive.
His eye was of black stone.
Let us leave aside whoever encountered him.
This was hardship itself,
They set out after riding at a trot,
Crossing the bloody marsh by night,
Calling it the dark eye of hardship,
There it lay fitted among the rocks,
A suffering people among the Kyrgyz nation,
Even the eyes that looked back,
Finding no mountain farther within,
Finding no enemy to fight,
One of them grew weary,
A fool who fled from labor,
Suited to what no eye could face,
Against the wrathful bloodshed,
Bound and given over as befitted them,
The poor twins fell into hardship,
The multitude drove them onward.
Their eyes read the signs of torment,
For snow there was only God,
They fought their way back through many lands,
There was no accustomed refuge in those lands,
It suited what they called Osh,
Believing him dead, his spirit sank,
The false world held countless men without arrows,
Lofty even amid evil,
The poor remnants who had strayed,
When the formidable host surrounded them,
Their extraordinary spirits sank,
Their soaked souls cried out,
The ravenous taker of souls,
As though reaching a hand into their shelter,
As though about to tear out their souls,
While they stood trembling in fear,
Blood drained away beneath God’s gaze,
Strength left the heroes,
Fearing disaster if they moved,
Hardship dimmed their failing eyes.
One ladle remained from all that was left,
Calling the humiliation within it humiliation,
Saying he should be freed from disgrace,
Those whose hearts could no longer endure,
What could not be was imposed again,
They descended from life in the place of honor,
Their faces turned pale,
As he stood speaking loudly like this,
Was it present within his grave?
He turned the seat of hell,
A fortress against four stratagems,
He cast light upon the company of nine,
He shared with those who had not divided,
He himself was among the divided,
O, toward the accursed one,
This was no mere word of Kenen,
Joining what had been severed,
Gathering what had been scattered,
Raising the dead back beside the living,
Making the blessing known,
Nurturing the poor,
Protecting the helpless,
That father burdened with grief,
His dark eyes watched in pursuit,
Sharing with those who had not divided,
It appeared that the children would remain,
To the sorrowful one who had arrived,
It was the moment to find a way,
A means remained amid the hardship,
His was a soul that stood ready to save,
The people bristled and waited,
A coat was drawn over his shoulders,
Calling him enemy, they cast him from life,
The wailing, destitute people,
A people fleeing from the wrathful one,
A people driven from their beloved souls,
Abandoning Talas and trampling onward.
Hardened beneath the world and sun,
The old man grazed his herd among the rocks,
Having both forbidden and lawful beasts slaughtered,
For the soul offered by the rich man,
Bringing his true weapon to bear,
Calling that people the enemy,
Calling the black hill his elder,
Setting a snare for the enemy people,
I am that old man,
If you look into his dark eyes,
If you ask where I dwell,
I am the dream of a wrathful man,
He entrusted it to the tiger-like hero,
The life sustained by one’s own hands,
Jelmayan at the farthest edge of the earth,
The foremost of swift travelers,
A saint’s coming upon the earth,
The cherished one of destiny,
The treasure found by the weeping old man,
The heroes awoke,
He said, “Forefather, it is I,”
Before the forefather’s dark eyes
A child met him with a cry,
Let us go to the valley,
Snow stung his eyes, and grief bound him,
Blood flowed from the extraordinary soul,
Let us go to his aid,
Following the trail of horse and faith,
Then, when they made for the valley,
From the world of the Kökötön spring,
Its bitter water and dense forest,
When the khan’s summer pasture fell into ruin,
Heedless of words from either side,
The offspring of the noble lion-hearted hero,
Did not heed that suffering was coming,
That treasure and its fellowship,
He did not heed the command to withdraw and go,
Ashamed when seen by other people.
Casting him aside,
I heard that he would abandon us and leave,
To the pain of the tormented heart,
Rolling through that night,
Bringing him toward the one who should come,
Turning restlessly in order to depart,
He became their leader,
At the center of Manas's host,
Between the two armies,
It was a river burning,
Its provision was its weapon,
The inheritance of every living person,
Entrusted to the river of Manas,
So grief would not lay a hand upon it,
So no soul would receive the news,
With a wrathful hand,
Until the end of the age,
So the curved lamp would not be taken,
So his soul would not go to the enemy,
The command of the Creator,
To submit to every punishment,
My warrior champion's bay horse,
Wearing his child at his waist,
Fate commanded it and spoke directly,
His thought grew within the heart,
May the people hold happiness in their hands,
The heart of Zhelzhetpes,
That he would leave before this,
The descendants of the white-capped Kyrgyz,
Separated from Ala-Too,
Scattered in their greatest hour,
Let him watch carefully and know the spring,
Let it not be said to be steel,
Rising and awakening from sleep,
The multitude gathered like hawks,
My dear champion fell,
In brief, you preserved him.
Thus spoke the holy man,
And reined in the charger,
Amid the people and the host,
His tidings could not be told by a thousand tongues,
Of the wrathful enemy,
He began speaking of their wickedness,
The one honored by the people was surrounded,
Calling them “my noble ones,” he spoke,
Amid a river of people,
Saying, “I am a hero,” he spoke,
And began the hero’s speech,
His soul stood high above the grave,
He had protected us poor wretches,
You yourself are a true holy man,
When he heard those words,
In the midst of the people’s host,
They bent their knees,
Running forward with greetings,
The nobly born man spoke softly,
Jeljetpes, eloquent Jeljetpes,
Began speaking to the holy man:
Let me compose my words, though strength has gone,
We come like wandering spirits,
There is no voice left even to utter a sound,
No people of our clan are near,
The people of Talas have no khan,
Their champions have no strength to fight,
We lay immersed in Quranic prayer,
In this red world we have no livestock,
Through the ages the world is refuse,
We come stripped of honor,
Cast into bitter lament,
Finding no forest in which to take shelter,
We come hungry and without a father.
Only one man’s strength remained,
The valiant Kyrgyz people remained.
The saint spread out his blessing.
This command gives the father to me.
Separated from the life held in trust,
He set the soles of his feet upon stone.
They burned Kenen beneath the sun.
No living soul remained among the captives.
Not one head of livestock remained at the station.
Our roots had not yet known sainthood.
Delivered into the hands of the faithless,
We reach the end in ruin.
Much humiliation and much lament,
We have endured in life.
When it flourished, we scattered it.
The day passed while we stood weeping.
We hurried away from the entrusted life.
Such was the state of his soul.
We froze in the cold and gave away our coats.
Saying “death,” we yielded our hands.
They brought his lips to food.
They clothed him for saddle and place of honor.
A form arose from what remained true.
Making the hero known,
They set it straight for the one who did not descend.
They sent him standing against the enemy.
They made him understand as though he knew nothing.
Thus they sent him into the enemy.
Remain as an elder brother.
We have seen wrath born of blood.
We are gray-maned lions.
Poor hero Kenen,
Immense one, spirit of God,
Many fists beat his restless wings.
They laid hands upon the khan’s daughter.
Her tongue, sweet as sugar, faltered.
The bosom of the cruel day,
These were brave Kenen’s words,
Before the one seated in the middle.
Before beads were hung before his eyes,
Before his fortune departed harshly,
For the soul whose destiny lay open,
From the beads that made one marvel,
The tortoise chewed that grass,
Countless wretches groaned from exhaustion,
Saying, “These are words spoken by destiny,”
Noble Jeljetpes began to speak,
When I spoke, these words arose,
Torment and hardship had awaited them,
Saying, “Elder, judge this somber day,”
If you are truly a holy hero,
He said, “Take heed of these precious words,”
From the honor beyond the open air,
Your spirit is like a god,
Saying, “Shake it like an egg,”
For the people beside the river,
A captive of white steel,
Descending from the lion-like steed,
The foremost one of the world,
The lion among the twin brothers,
The son of the hero Kyrgyz,
The son of heroic Kenen the lion,
Who struck ninety men in a crowd,
Whose kindred names were made to rhyme,
The Talas plain rich in livestock,
The son of hero Kenen,
Giant Kulan and the two lion-hearted heroes,
Who saw the torment of that broken day,
